executive_briefing: The international tax landscape remains highly dynamic, dominated by the ongoing, widespread implementation of Pillar Two, establishing a 15% global minimum corporate tax, and the US's continued distinctive 'side-by-side arrangement,' which subjects its MNEs to domestic minimum taxes with specific tax code interactions. Concurrently, global trade is navigating a resurgence of protectionist tariffs, notably in the US, marked by ongoing legal challenges, recent court rulings affecting past tariffs, and the announcement of new trade measures, fueling significant supply chain uncertainty. Beyond these major shifts, jurisdictions globally are independently adjusting corporate and withholding tax rates. Regionally, Singapore reinforces its attractive 17% corporate tax rate and one-tier system, supported by its evolving multi-year InvoiceNow/Peppol e-invoicing mandate, exemplifying the broader global movement towards digital tax transformation and standardized e-invoicing.

trends.name: Global Minimum Corporate Tax (Pillar Two) and US Divergence
trends.summary: The OECD's Pillar Two establishes a 15% global minimum corporate tax rate for large MNEs, with over 140 jurisdictions enforcing the rules. As of January 2026, 147 countries and jurisdictions within the OECD Inclusive Framework agreed to a 'side-by-side arrangement' that exempts US-headquartered companies from direct Pillar Two rules, subjecting them to US global minimum taxes instead, with specific interactions for domestic tax code provisions like NCTI, BEAT, FDDEI, and R&D expensing, in addition to the Undertaxed Profits Rule (UTPR). This represents a global shift in tax philosophy, with ongoing implementation efforts like Australia's Taxation Rules 2024.
trends.evidence: Over 140 jurisdictions are enforcing Pillar Two rules as of January 2026, establishing a 15% global minimum effective tax rate. In January 2026, the OECD Inclusive Framework agreed to a 'side-by-side arrangement' accommodating US objections, where US-headquartered companies remain subject to US global minimum taxes while exempted from Pillar Two. This arrangement includes interactions with US tax code provisions such as NCTI, BEAT, FDDEI, and R&D expensing. The Undertaxed Profits Rule (UTPR) is a key component of this global tax deal. Australia, for instance, issued the Taxation (Multinational—Global and Domestic Minimum Tax) Rules 2024 on December 23, 2024, for Pillar 2 GloBE rules. This framework aims to ensure MNEs pay a minimum level of tax and limit incentives for profit shifting, marking a global shift in tax philosophy.

trends.name: Resurgence of Trade Tariffs
trends.summary: The US is actively implementing and considering new tariffs, creating significant disruptions to global trade and supply chains. Recent actions in April 2026 included updates to Section 232 tariffs on key metals and new measures targeting pharmaceutical imports, alongside broader tariffs on key trading partners. This trend is highly dynamic, marked by ongoing legal challenges, including a US Supreme Court review of IEEPA tariffs and a US trade court ruling in favor of businesses, leading to refunds for some importers and the announcement of new Section 122 tariffs, alongside the potential for renewed reciprocal tariffs.
trends.evidence: In April 2026, the U.S. made significant updates to Section 232 tariffs for key metals (steel, aluminum, copper, etc.) and introduced new tariff measures targeting pharmaceutical imports. New US tariffs have also been announced, including 25% on most imports from Canada, Mexico, and China, and 10% on Canadian energy, with global steel/aluminum tariffs anticipated. Tariffs are taxes on imported goods paid by companies to the government, creating additional costs. The U.S. Supreme Court is expected to rule on the legality of past tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), which are now being refunded to importers. Following a SCOTUS decision, the White House announced Section 122 tariffs for 150 days. Additionally, a US trade court ruled in favor of small businesses challenging tariffs under a 1970s trade law. The US International Trade Commission (USITC) provides analysis, and tracking of implemented US tariffs and counter-tariffs from other countries is ongoing.

trends.name: Singapore E-invoicing (InvoiceNow/Peppol PINT SG) Mandate
trends.summary: Singapore's nationwide e-invoicing initiative, InvoiceNow, is progressing as a multiyear mandate for structured invoice data submission to IRAS, built on the global Peppol interoperability framework. Reaffirmed in March 2026, this initiative is becoming a core component of Singapore's digital tax transformation, streamlining payment cycles, improving efficiency, and expanding its scope to include more GST-registered businesses with phased deadlines. Singapore, a pioneer in ASEAN e-invoicing, is driving a government-led shift away from paper invoices toward structured electronic document exchange.
trends.evidence: InvoiceNow, based on the Peppol framework, has evolved into a multiyear mandate requiring structured invoice data submission to the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore (IRAS), as confirmed in March 2026. The Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) has developed this Nationwide E-invoicing Network, with IMDA being the first Peppol Authority outside of Europe. The initiative streamlines payment cycles and improves efficiency by enabling direct exchange of invoice data in a structured digital format, with phased deadlines announced in February 2026 expanding mandatory participation to existing GST-registered businesses. Singapore's e-invoicing requirements for 2026 represent a government-driven shift away from paper and PDF invoices, with the country being a pioneer in the ASEAN region for electronic document exchange since 2018. This framework supports seamless exchange across both Peppol and non-Peppol channels.

trends.name: Singapore Competitive Corporate Tax Environment
trends.summary: Singapore continues to offer a highly competitive corporate tax environment with a stable 17% rate, enhanced by attractive exemptions, rebates (including for income year 2025/year of assessment 2026), and a one-tier taxation system where dividends are tax-exempt. This strategic approach, coupled with its territorial tax system where resident companies are taxed on local and remitted foreign profits, solidifies its appeal for foreign investment and global businesses, boasting the lowest corporate tax rate in ASEAN.
trends.evidence: Singapore's corporate income tax rate remains at 17% for both local and foreign companies, which is the lowest in ASEAN. It employs a one-tier taxation system where dividends are tax-exempt for shareholders, simplifying the tax code and reducing compliance costs. For income year 2025 (year of assessment 2026), eligible companies will receive a non-taxable CIT rebate cash grant of SGD 2,000, and all companies will be granted a 50% CIT rebate, capped at SGD 40,000 (or SGD 38,000 if qualifying for the cash grant). The headline rate is 17%, but most companies pay a lower effective rate due to these exemptions, incentives, and periodic rebates. Singapore uses a territorial tax system, taxing resident companies on profits derived in Singapore and foreign profits remitted to Singapore.

trends.name: ASEAN Diverse Corporate Tax Landscape
trends.summary: The ASEAN region presents a highly diverse corporate tax landscape characterized by varying rates, exemptions, and digital tax adoption approaches, significantly influencing investment decisions and raising concerns about tax competition and harmonization. While Singapore maintains a competitive edge with its 17% rate, countries like Cambodia, Brunei, and Thailand have rates around 20%. Several ASEAN+3 economies are actively reviewing and amending domestic laws to align with global minimum tax (Pillar Two) requirements, alongside varied VAT/GST implementations.
trends.evidence: Corporate tax rates vary significantly across ASEAN nations, with Singapore at 17% (the lowest in ASEAN) and countries like Cambodia, Brunei, and Thailand at 20%. This diversity influences tax competition and harmonization efforts within the region. Several ASEAN+3 economies have initiated reviews and amendments to their domestic laws to apply a top-up tax to meet Pillar Two's 15% effective corporate income tax rate for large MNEs. The region also shows variation in consumption taxes, with Singapore and Malaysia using GST, and Brunei having no VAT. Research indicates ongoing discussions regarding tax competition and harmonization in ASEAN.

trends.name: Global Corporate Tax Rate Adjustments
trends.summary: Beyond global minimum tax initiatives, numerous jurisdictions are implementing independent changes to their corporate income tax rates for 2026, including both increases and decreases, alongside adjustments to withholding taxes. These widespread legislative changes, applying from January 1, 2026, underscore a dynamic global tax environment requiring continuous monitoring and careful business planning.
trends.evidence: Corporate and withholding tax rate changes are applying from January 1, 2026, across various jurisdictions. These changes are independent of global minimum tax initiatives, with examples including Portugal's corporate income tax decreasing by one percentage point per year from January 2026 until 2028, and Slovenia's top corporate income tax temporarily increasing from 19% to 22% for five years. The UAE also introduced a federal corporate tax law in December 2022. Global tracking of statutory Corporate Income Tax (CIT) rates across territories indicates continuous adjustments.

trends.name: Digital Tax Transformation: E-invoicing Standardization
trends.summary: The global trend towards digital tax transformation is accelerating, with a growing emphasis on e-invoicing as a standardized method for electronic billing. This involves the electronic presentation and exchange of transactional documents (like invoices, purchase orders, debit/credit notes) in structured data formats (e.g., EDI, XML). E-invoicing incorporates descriptive tax data to meet domestic and international financial reporting standards, leading to improved compliance, efficiency, cost savings, and faster payment cycles through validation on designated portals.
trends.evidence: E-invoicing, an umbrella term for electronic billing, encompasses various technologies like Electronic Data Interchange (EDI) and XML data file formats for transmitting structured information. It is designed to include descriptive tax data to comply with government standards for financial reporting, streamline invoice management, reduce errors, speed approvals, and improve compliance for transactional documents between trade partners, with implementations occurring as recently as April 2026. This global shift aims for cost savings, improved accuracy, sustainability, and enhanced compliance. Under this concept, B2B invoices issued by a taxpayer are often required to be validated on a designated Invoice Registration Portal (IRP), facilitating the electronic exchange of invoices between buyer and seller.
